segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For as to the service for the holy ones, it is superfluous for me to write to you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for I know your eagerness, which I boast about on your behalf to the Macedonians, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year; and your zeal has stirred up most of them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I am sending the brothers so that our boast about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, just as I kept saying you would be;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: otherwise, if any Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—not to mention you—would be put to shame in this undertaking.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and prepare in advance the bounty you promised beforehand, so that it may be ready as a bounty and not as something extorted.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Each of you should give as you have decided in your heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And God is able to make all grace overflow to you, so that, having all you need in all things at all times, you may overflow in every good work.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the one who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed and increase the harvest of your righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You will be enriched in every way for every kind of generosity, which through us produces thanksgiving to God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because the service of this public offering is not only supplying what the holy ones lack but is also overflowing through many thanksgivings to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Through the proof this service gives, they will glorify God for the obedience that comes with your confession of the good news of Christ and for the generosity of your sharing with them and with everyone,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and in their prayer for you they long for you because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift!

notes.note: The Greek word is an ordinary term for service rendered or a task carried out on someone's behalf; 'ministry' now suggests a church office or profession. Here it refers to the collection of money Paul was organising among his largely non-Jewish congregations for the impoverished believers in Jerusalem, the subject of chapters 8 and 9.

The traditional 'saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Paul uses the word for all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel; here it means specifically the believers in Jerusalem. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

Older translations, and several current ones, render this 'in this confidence' or 'for being so confident'. The standard modern lexicon argues that the sense 'confidence' is not securely attested for this word in the period, and that it means here a plan, project or undertaking (or, on another view, 'situation'). Some recent translations already read 'undertaking'; the matter remains disputed.

The Greek word normally means 'blessing' and is used here for a gift given freely and generously. The same word returns in verse 6, literally 'sows on the basis of blessings', which is why 'bounty' and 'bountifully' are used to keep Paul's link between the two verses.

The word means greed, the desire to have more. It may refer to greed on the collectors' side, so that the gift would look like money squeezed out of the Corinthians (the reading followed here), or to a grasping spirit in the givers, yielding 'not as something grudgingly given'. Both readings have scholarly support.

This echoes a line found in the Greek version of Proverbs 22:8 but absent from the Hebrew text: 'God blesses a cheerful and giving man.' That same verse of Proverbs speaks of sowing and reaping, the image Paul has just used.

Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice). The quotation is from Psalm 112:9, where the one who gives to the poor is the person who fears the Lord, and 'righteousness' is right conduct shown in generosity; in Jewish usage of the period the word could come close to meaning charitable giving. Some interpreters think Paul takes God as the subject of the quotation.

The word's basic sense is singleness or sincerity: giving without reserve or ulterior motive. Most translations render it 'generosity' here and in verse 13 because of the context, but some lexicographers hold that 'sincere, wholehearted concern' is sufficient in every occurrence. The difference is one of emphasis: the open spirit of the giving versus its amount.

Traditional versions have 'the administration (or ministry) of this service', which blurs two different Greek words. This one was the term in Greek cities for a public service that a citizen undertook at his own expense, and in the Septuagint for the service of priests in the sanctuary. Paul presents the collection as both a civic-style benefaction and an act of worship; 'public offering' attempts to carry both.

The Greek has only a participle, 'glorifying God', with no stated subject. Most interpreters take the recipients in Jerusalem as those who praise God because of the Corinthians' obedience, which fits verse 14; others take the Corinthians as the subject ('you glorify God by your obedience'). The grammar of verses 11–14 is loose and allows either.

'Gospel' has become a religious term or the name of a kind of book. The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between 'gospel' and 'good news'.

The word translated 'Thanks' is the same Greek word translated 'grace' in verses 8 and 14; it covers both a favour freely given and the gratitude it calls forth. Paul closes the whole discussion of the collection, in which this word has recurred throughout chapters 8 and 9, by returning grace to God as thanks.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout the New Testament in the senses favour, gift, grace and thanks, and chapters 8–9 play on all of them, so the split between renderings needs one policy.
Translators vary between ministry, service, relief and administration across the letters and Acts, and 'ministry' now misleads towards a clerical office.
The traditional 'confidence' is lexically doubtful, and the word recurs in 2 Corinthians 11:17 and Hebrews 1:3, 3:14 and 11:1, where the choice of sense is theologically weighty.
Rendered variously as fellowship, communion, participation, contribution and sharing across the New Testament; readers lose the connection unless one policy is set.
Lexicographers dispute whether it ever means generosity or always sincerity/singleness; it recurs in Romans 12:8, 2 Corinthians 1:12, 8:2 and 11:3, Ephesians 6:5 and Colossians 3:22.
